title: II. The Alarm
paragraphs: Our police captain, Mihail Makarovitch Makarov, a retired lieutenant colonel, was a widower and an excellent man. He had only come to us three years before, but he had won general esteem, chiefly because he “knew how to keep society together.” He was never without visitors and couldn't have got along without them. Someone was always dining with him; he never sat down to table without guests. He gave regular dinners too, on all sorts of occasions, sometimes very surprising ones. Though the food wasn't _recherché_, it was abundant. The fish pies were excellent, and the wine made up in quantity for what it lacked in quality.

The first room his guests entered was a well-fitted billiard room, with pictures of English race-horses in black frames on the walls—an essential decoration, as we all know, for a bachelor's billiard room. There was card-playing every evening at his house, even if only at one table. But at frequent intervals, all the society of our town, with the mammas and young ladies, gathered at his house to dance. Though Mihail Makarovitch was a widower, he didn't live alone. His widowed daughter lived with him, with her two unmarried daughters—grown-up girls who had finished their education. They had an agreeable appearance and a lively character, and though everyone knew they would have no dowry, they attracted all the fashionable young men to their grandfather's house.

Mihail Makarovitch was by no means very efficient in his work, though he performed his duties no worse than many others. To speak plainly, he was a man of rather narrow education. His understanding of the limits of his administrative power could not always be relied on. It wasn't so much that he failed to grasp certain reforms passed during the present reign, as that he made conspicuous blunders in interpreting them. This wasn't from any special lack of intelligence, but from carelessness—he was always in too great a hurry to really go into the subject.

“I have the heart of a soldier rather than of a civilian,” he used to say of himself. He hadn't even formed a definite idea of the fundamental principles of the reforms connected with the emancipation of the serfs, and only picked it up, so to speak, from year to year, involuntarily increasing his knowledge by practice. And yet he was himself a landowner. Pyotr Ilyitch knew for certain that he would meet some of Mihail Makarovitch's visitors there that evening, but he didn't know which ones. As it happened, at that moment the prosecutor and Varvinsky, our district doctor—a young man who had only just come to us from Petersburg after taking a brilliant degree at the Academy of Medicine—were playing whist at the police captain's. Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor (he was really the deputy prosecutor, but we always called him the prosecutor), was a rather peculiar man, about thirty-five, inclined to be consumptive, and married to a fat, childless woman. He was vain and irritable, though he had a good intellect, and even a kind heart. It seemed the only thing wrong with him was that he had a higher opinion of himself than his ability warranted. And that made him seem constantly uneasy. He also had certain higher, even artistic, leanings—toward psychology, for instance, a special study of the human heart, a particular knowledge of the criminal and his crime. He nursed a grievance on this ground, feeling he had been passed over in the service, and firmly convinced that in higher spheres he had not been properly appreciated and had enemies. In gloomy moments he even threatened to give up his post and practice as a barrister in criminal cases. The unexpected Karamazov case agitated him profoundly: “It was a case that might well be talked about all over Russia.” But I am getting ahead of myself.

Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov, the young investigating lawyer, who had come from Petersburg only two months earlier, was sitting in the next room with the young ladies. People talked about it afterwards and wondered at how all the gentlemen, as if intentionally, on the evening of “the crime,” had been gathered together at the house of the executive authority. Yet it was perfectly simple and happened quite naturally.

Ippolit Kirillovitch's wife had had a toothache for the last two days, and he was obliged to go out to escape her groans. The doctor, by the very nature of his being, couldn't spend an evening anywhere but at cards. Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov had been planning for three days now to drop in that evening at Mihail Makarovitch's, so to speak casually, so as slyly to startle the eldest granddaughter, Olga Mihailovna, by showing he knew her secret—that he knew it was her birthday, and that she was trying to conceal it on purpose, so as not to be obliged to give a dance. He anticipated a great deal of merriment, many playful jests about her age and her being afraid to reveal it, about his knowing her secret and telling everybody, and so on. The charming young man was a great adept at such teasing; the ladies had christened him “the naughty man,” and he seemed delighted with the name. He was extremely well-bred, however, of good family, education, and feelings, and though he led a life of pleasure, his sallies were always innocent and in good taste. He was short and delicate-looking. On his white, slender little fingers he always wore a number of big, glittering rings. When he was engaged in his official duties, he always became extraordinarily grave, as though he was conscious of his position and the sanctity of the obligations laid on him. He had a special gift for mystifying murderers and other criminals of the peasant class during interrogation, and if he didn't win their respect, he certainly succeeded in arousing their wonder.

Pyotr Ilyitch was simply dumbfounded when he walked into the police captain's. He saw instantly that everyone already knew. They had actually thrown down their cards; all were standing and talking. Even Nikolay Parfenovitch had left the young ladies and come running in, looking strenuous and ready for action. Pyotr Ilyitch was met with the astounding news that old Fyodor Pavlovitch really had been murdered that evening in his own house—murdered and robbed. The news had only just reached them, in the following way.

Marfa Ignatyevna, the wife of old Grigory, who had been knocked senseless near the fence, was sleeping soundly in her bed and might well have slept till morning after the draught she'd taken. But all at once she woke up, no doubt roused by a fearful epileptic scream from Smerdyakov, who was lying in the next room unconscious. That scream always came before his fits, and always terrified and upset Marfa Ignatyevna. She could never get used to it. She jumped up and ran half-awake to Smerdyakov's room. But it was dark there, and all she could hear was the invalid beginning to gasp and struggle. Then Marfa Ignatyevna herself screamed out and was about to call her husband, when she suddenly realized that when she had got up, he wasn't beside her in bed. She ran back to the bedstead and began groping with her hands, but the bed really was empty. Then he must have gone out—where? She ran to the steps and timidly called to him. She got no answer, of course, but she did catch the sound of groans far away in the garden in the darkness. She listened. The groans were repeated, and it was clear they came from the garden.
“Good Lord! Just as it was with Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya!” she thought distractedly. She went timidly down the steps and saw that the gate into the garden was open.
“He must be out there, poor dear,” she thought. She went up to the gate and all at once she distinctly heard Grigory calling her by name, “Marfa! Marfa!” in a weak, moaning, dreadful voice.

“Lord, preserve us from harm!” Marfa Ignatyevna murmured, and ran toward the voice, and that was how she found Grigory. But she found him not by the fence where he had been knocked down, but about twenty paces off. It turned out later that he had crawled away after coming to himself, and had probably been a long time getting that far, losing consciousness several times along the way. She noticed at once that he was covered in blood, and screamed at the top of her voice. Grigory was muttering incoherently:
“He has murdered—his father murdered. Why scream, silly—run—fetch someone—”

But Marfa kept on screaming, and seeing that her master's window was open and that there was a candle lit in it, she ran over and began calling for Fyodor Pavlovitch. But as she peered through the window, she saw a fearful sight. Her master was lying on his back, motionless, on the floor. His light-colored dressing gown and white shirt were soaked with blood. The candle on the table brightly lit up the blood and the motionless dead face of Fyodor Pavlovitch. Terror-stricken, Marfa rushed away from the window, ran out of the garden, drew the bolt of the big gate, and ran headlong by the back way to the neighbor, Marya Kondratyevna. Both mother and daughter were asleep, but they woke at Marfa's desperate, persistent screaming and knocking at the shutter. Marfa, shrieking and screaming incoherently, managed to tell them the main fact and to beg for help. As it happened, Foma had come back from his wanderings and was staying the night with them. They got him up at once, and all three ran to the scene of the crime. On the way, Marya Kondratyevna remembered that at about eight o'clock she had heard a dreadful scream from their garden, and this was no doubt Grigory's cry, “Parricide!”—uttered when he caught hold of Mitya's leg.

“One person screamed out and then was silent,” Marya Kondratyevna explained as she ran. When they reached the place where Grigory lay, the two women, with Foma's help, carried him to the lodge. They lit a candle and saw that Smerdyakov was no better, that he was writhing in convulsions, his eyes fixed in a squint, and that foam was flowing from his lips. They moistened Grigory's forehead with water mixed with vinegar, and the water revived him at once. He asked immediately:
“Is the master murdered?”

Then Foma and both women ran to the house and saw this time that not only the window but also the door into the garden was wide open, though for the past week Fyodor Pavlovitch had locked himself in every night and wouldn't let even Grigory come in on any pretext. Seeing that door open, they were afraid to go in to Fyodor Pavlovitch “for fear anything should happen afterwards.” When they got back to Grigory, the old man told them to go straight to the police captain. Marya Kondratyevna ran there and raised the alarm with the whole party at the police captain's. She arrived only five minutes before Pyotr Ilyitch, so that his story came not as his own surmise and theory, but as the direct confirmation, by a witness, of the theory they all held about the identity of the criminal (a theory he had, in the bottom of his heart, refused to believe until that moment).

It was decided to act with energy. The deputy police inspector of the town was assigned to take four witnesses, enter Fyodor Pavlovitch's house, and open an inquiry on the spot according to the regular procedures, which I will not go into here. The district doctor, a zealous man, new to his work, practically insisted on accompanying the police captain, the prosecutor, and the investigating lawyer.

I will note briefly that Fyodor Pavlovitch was found to be quite dead, with his skull battered in. But with what? Most likely the same weapon with which Grigory had been attacked. And as soon as that weapon was found, Grigory—who was now given every possible medical assistance—described in a weak, breaking voice how he had been knocked down. They began searching with a lantern by the fence and found the brass pestle dropped in a most conspicuous place on the garden path. There were no signs of disturbance in the room where Fyodor Pavlovitch was lying. But by the bed, behind the screen, they picked up from the floor a big, thick envelope inscribed: “A present of three thousand roubles for my angel Grushenka, if she is willing to come.” And below, Fyodor Pavlovitch had added, “For my little chicken.” There were three seals of red sealing-wax on the envelope, but it had been torn open and was empty: the money had been removed. They also found on the floor a piece of narrow pink ribbon with which the envelope had been tied.

One piece of Pyotr Ilyitch's evidence made a great impression on the prosecutor and the investigating magistrate—namely, his idea that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would shoot himself before daybreak, that he had resolved to do so, had spoken of it to Ilyitch, had taken the pistols, loaded them in front of him, written a letter, put it in his pocket, and so on. When Pyotr Ilyitch, though still unwilling to believe in it, had threatened to tell someone in order to prevent the suicide, Mitya had answered with a grin: “You'll be too late.” So they had to hurry to Mokroe to find the criminal before he really did shoot himself.
“That's clear, that's clear!” the prosecutor kept repeating in great excitement. “That's just the way with mad fellows like that: ‘I'll kill myself tomorrow, so I'll make merry till I die!'”
The story of how he had bought the wine and provisions excited the prosecutor more than ever.

“Do you remember the fellow who murdered a merchant called Olsufyev, gentlemen? He stole fifteen hundred, went straight off to have his hair curled, and then, without even hiding the money, carrying it almost in his hand in just the same way, he went off to the girls.”

They were all delayed, however, by the inquiry, the search, the formalities, and so on, at Fyodor Pavlovitch's house. It all took time, and so, two hours before setting out, they sent on ahead to Mokroe the officer of the rural police, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch Schmertsov, who had arrived in town the morning before to collect his pay. He was instructed to avoid raising the alarm when he reached Mokroe, but to keep constant watch over the “criminal” until the proper authorities arrived, and also to secure witnesses for the arrest, police constables, and so on. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch did as he was told, preserving his incognito and giving no one but his old acquaintance Trifon Borissovitch the slightest hint of his secret business. He had spoken to him just before Mitya met the landlord on the balcony, looking for him in the dark, and Mitya had at once noticed a change in Trifon Borissovitch's face and voice. So neither Mitya nor anyone else knew that he was being watched. The box with the pistols had been carried off by Trifon Borissovitch and put in a suitable place. Only after four o'clock, almost at sunrise, did all the officials—the police captain, the prosecutor, the investigating lawyer—drive up in two carriages, each drawn by three horses. The doctor stayed behind at Fyodor Pavlovitch's to perform a post-mortem on the body the next day. But he was particularly interested in the condition of the servant, Smerdyakov.

“Such violent and prolonged epileptic fits, recurring continually for twenty-four hours, are rarely met with and are of interest to science,” he declared enthusiastically to his companions, and as they left they laughingly congratulated him on his find. The prosecutor and the investigating lawyer distinctly remembered the doctor's saying that Smerdyakov could not outlive the night.
After these long but, I think, necessary explanations, we will return to the point in our tale where we left off.
